title: Couscous: the dish that united the Maghreb
subtitle: In 2020, Algeria, Mauritania, Morocco and Tunisia set aside closed borders and diplomatic rifts to submit a shared recipe to UNESCO.

parts.text: For decades, political relations across North Africa's Maghreb have been marked by closed land borders, diplomatic standoffs, and sharp disagreements over regional sovereignty.

In December 2020, four neighboring states — Algeria, Mauritania, Morocco, and Tunisia — achieved an unprecedented diplomatic consensus by jointly inscribing the knowledge, know-how, and practices of couscous on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage List.
Rather than claiming exclusive national ownership over the dish, the joint file celebrated couscous as a living cultural bond that transcends national borders.

sections.title: The invention of the steam pot

parts.text: Culinary historians trace the origins of couscous directly to the indigenous Berber (Imazighen) populations of North Africa.

Archaeological excavations in Numidian burial sites dating back to the reign of King Massinissa (3rd to 2nd century BCE) uncovered pierced ceramic vessels functionally identical to modern couscoussier steamers.

The fundamental culinary breakthrough of couscous was technological: rolling coarse hard durum wheat semolina with salt water into uniform granules, drying them in the sun, and cooking them suspended above boiling broth in a perforated pot (keskas), rather than boiling the grain directly in water as a gruel.

In every country of the Maghreb, couscous remains the defining meal of Friday prayers and family reconciliations. Traditionally served in a wide earthenware bowl (gsaa or tebsi), it is eaten together from the center using spoons or rolled into small morsels with three fingers of the right hand.

sections.title: One dish, a thousand regional identities

parts.text: While the steaming method is shared, each region developed distinct signatures.

On the Tunisian coast and the island of Djerba, couscous is perfumed with red mullet, grouper, and fiery harissa; in the Moroccan imperial cities of Fes and Marrakech, festive versions feature 'Tfaya', a sweet garnish of caramelized onions, raisins, and cinnamon over lamb; while in Algerian highlands, stews favor turnips, chickpeas, zucchini, and peppery saffron broth.

gaps: Scholars dispute whether millet or durum wheat was the original cereal used for early pre-Islamic couscous rolling in the western Sahara.

The degree to which the trans-Saharan caravan routes carried couscous techniques southward into West Africa (where fonio and sorghum are steamed similarly) is documented in few surviving medieval Arabic travelogues.

keyPoints.text: In 2020, Algeria, Mauritania, Morocco, and Tunisia jointly inscribed couscous on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage List.
Archaeological evidence confirms that pierced ceramic couscous steamers originated with indigenous Berber civilizations over 2,000 years ago.
The dish is defined by the technique of gentle steam-cooking above a simmering broth, serving as a social peacemaker across North Africa.
